title: Contagious Interview
summary: Contagious Interview is a financially and strategically motivated intrusion set tracked publicly under the aliases DeceptiveDevelopment, Gwisin Gang, Tenacious Pungsan, DEV#POPPER, PurpleBravo and TAG-121, with several of those names describing overlapping clusters rather than one proven single organisation. Public reporting attributes the activity to North Korean interests, and much of it is described as tied to the wider scheme of placing information technology workers in foreign companies. The tradecraft is social engineering rather than exploitation: operators pose as recruiters on professional networks and chat apps, move the conversation to a coding exercise or a debugging task, and hand the target a repository or archive carrying a trojanised loader. Payload families seen in reporting include JavaScript and Python stealer and remote access components that run on the developer workstation, collect browser credentials, cryptocurrency wallet data and files, and maintain a command and control channel. Because no vulnerability is used, evidence sits in email and messaging gateways, in shell and interpreter history, in process ancestry where a code editor or interpreter spawns a shell, and in outbound connections to lookalike recruitment or package hosting domains.

beginner.definition: Contagious Interview is the public name for a group of attackers who pretend to be recruiters. They offer you a job interview or a coding test. Then they ask you to run their code on your own computer, and that code steals your data. Other security companies use different names for the same activity.
beginner.whyItMatters: Software developers keep valuable access on their work laptops. If you run a stranger's project, the attacker can steal passwords, source code and cloud keys. This group is hard to catch because they never break in. You invite them in yourself, which means the usual defences may stay quiet.
howItWorks: The attacker finds you on a job site or a chat app and offers a role or a contract.
They move the talk to a chat app and send a friendly coding test or a project link.
The project contains a hidden file that downloads more code when you build or run it.
That code runs quietly in the background on your work computer and your home computer.
It gathers passwords, browser sessions, wallet files and documents, then sends them out.
The attacker keeps a hidden channel open to send new orders later.
beginner.example: Imagine a stranger at a bus stop offers you a well paid job. The interview is simple, they say. Just install this small app on your phone so we can check your skills. The app looks normal, and it even works. In the background it copies your messages and your bank app, and sends them to the stranger. Nothing was broken into. You opened the door yourself, and that is exactly why Contagious Interview works.
takeaways: A real employer never needs you to run untrusted code on your own machine before hiring you.
Interview software should run in a separate, disposable computer or a sandbox, never on your daily laptop.
If you already ran something suspicious, tell your security team fast and change your passwords.

objectives: Explain how fake recruitment social engineering leads to code execution on a developer workstation.
Describe the stages of a Contagious Interview intrusion from first contact to data theft.
Recognise the warning signs of a fraudulent recruiter or a hostile coding challenge.
Identify the endpoint and network evidence such an intrusion leaves behind.
Suggest practical controls that protect developers who receive unsolicited job offers.
State plainly which parts of the attribution to this cluster remain uncertain.
